cases.title: Mt. Etna Object
cases.summary: In December 2018, a forward-looking infrared video sensor aboard an uncrewed U.S. Air Force platform captured this footage while operating over the Mediterranean Sea. This footage depicts an object that appears to be transiting a plume of superheated gas and ash produced by an eruption of Mt. Etna, a volcano in Sicily, Italy. AARO coordinated an interagency and international analytical effort that determined that optical effects from the intense atmospheric conditions near the volcano distorted the video, causing the object to appear to transit the plume. AARO assesses with moderate confidence that the footage instead depicts a balloon approximately 170 kilometers from the caldera traveling at wind speed and direction.

cases.summary: On April 26, 2013, an infrared sensor onboard a U.S. Customs and Border Protection aircraft captured footage of a UAP event over the Rafael Hernandez Airport near Aguadilla, Puerto Rico. The footage appears to depict a UAP moving at high speed, splitting into two objects, and entering and exiting the water before disappearing into the ocean off Puerto Rico's northwestern coast. AARO assesses with high confidence that the objects did not demonstrate anomalous speeds or flight behaviors. An Intelligence Community partner's reconstruction of the flight path and look angle from the infrared sensor indicates that the video instead depicts two objects traveling near each other rather than a single object splitting into two. This reconstruction also demonstrates that the objects traveled in a straight line at wind speed and did not enter the water at any point.

files.title: 2013 Puerto Rico Object Reconstruction
files.description: This video shows a Systems Toolkit digital reconstruction of "The Puerto Rico Object" unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) event as seen from above. The reconstruction shows the aircraft's flight path, an onboard infrared sensor’s look angle to the ground, and the objects’ assessed flight path. This reconstruction demonstrates that the objects traveled in a straight line at wind speed over land. On April 26, 2013, an infrared sensor onboard a U.S. Customs and Border Protection aircraft captured footage of a UAP event over the Rafael Hernandez Airport near Aguadilla, Puerto Rico. AARO assesses with high confidence that the objects did not demonstrate anomalous speeds or flight behaviors.

files.title: Al Taqaddum Object
files.description: In October 2017, an infrared sensor onboard a force protection aerostat near Al Taqaddum Air Base, Iraq, captured 17 minutes of video of an unidentified object. AARO assesses that the object was a cluster of partially and fully inflated balloons. The object's appearance is consistent with other recorded observations featuring balloon clusters. AARO employed full-motion video analysis and pixel examination techniques to inform its assessment. AARO assesses that the object did not demonstrate anomalous performance characteristics. AARO used geo-locational data from the aerostat to assess the object's speed and direction of travel.

files.title: Middle East Red Balloon 2024
files.description: The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office received a report from a U.S. military Service consisting of one minute and thirty-six seconds of full-motion video footage captured by a camera aboard a U.S. military platform in the Middle East in 2024. According to the reporting Service, the recording likely depicts a slow-moving spheroidal object. AARO assesses, with high confidence, that the object depicted in the video is almost certainly (≥95% likelihood) a consumer-grade reflective foil balloon. AARO bases its assessment on the object's strong morphological consistency with other resolved imagery depicting balloons and its behavioral correlation with recorded wind speed and direction during the event.

files.title: Mt. Etna Object
files.description: In December 2018, a forward-looking infrared video sensor aboard an uncrewed U.S. Air Force platform captured this footage while operating over the Mediterranean Sea. This footage depicts an object that appears to be transiting a plume of superheated gas and ash produced by an eruption of Mt. Etna, a volcano in Sicily, Italy. AARO coordinated an interagency and international analytical effort that determined that optical effects from the intense atmospheric conditions near the volcano distorted the video, causing the object to appear to transit the plume. AARO assesses with moderate confidence that the footage instead depicts a balloon approximately 170 kilometers from the caldera traveling at wind speed and direction.

files.title: Puerto Rico Objects
files.description: On April 26, 2013, an infrared sensor onboard a U.S. Customs and Border Protection aircraft captured footage of a UAP event over the Rafael Hernandez Airport near Aguadilla, Puerto Rico. The footage appears to depict a UAP moving at high speed, splitting into two objects, and entering and exiting the water before disappearing into the ocean off Puerto Rico's northwestern coast. AARO assesses with high confidence that the objects did not demonstrate anomalous speeds or flight behaviors. An Intelligence Community partner's reconstruction of the flight path and look angle from the infrared sensor indicates that the video instead depicts two objects traveling near each other rather than a single object splitting into two. This reconstruction also demonstrates that the objects traveled in a straight line at wind speed and did not enter the water at any point.

files.description: An Apollo 12 air-to-ground voice transcript from 1969, included in the NASA UAP document release. The UAP-relevant passage is the crew discussing small "bits and pieces" floating alongside the spacecraft: on an earlier nightside pass the tracking light was seen flashing off these particles, and the commander uses their continued presence to deduce the tracking light has burned out.

The transcript records crew chatter, not an investigation; the particles are discussed as ordinary spacecraft debris.

findings.title: Source records are not proof of origin

findings.title: Historical records provide context, not continuity
findings.summary: The crawl includes roughly 7 historically dated groups and 56 modern groups. Historical military, FBI, NASA, and State Department records help track vocabulary and public concern, but should not be treated as evidence of one continuous phenomenon without case-level corroboration.

findings.title: The release mixes modern sensor cases with historical scans

findings.title: Unresolved does not mean extraordinary

official_records.title: Black and White Photographs of U.S. Air Force and Predecessors' Activities, Facilities, and Personnel, Domestic and Foreign
official_records.creator: Department of Defense. Department of the Air Force. 9/26/1947-
official_records.summary: The approximately 180,000 black and white negatives in this series correspond to prints in Record Group 342, Series FH ("Black and White and Color Photographs of U.S. Air Force and Predecessor Agencies Activities, Facilities and Personnel - World War II and Korean War") and Series B ("Black and White and Color Photographs of U.S. Air Force Activities, Facilities and Personnel, Domestic and Foreign"). Negatives in this series appear in two groups- some 154,000 housed in large (8 1/2"x11" or 9"x11") jackets, and some 26,000 housed in small (4 1/2"x5 1/2") jackets. The jacket size does not necessarily indicate negative size, since a majority of the negatives in the large jackets are in fact 4"x5" or smaller. A single numerical sequence spans both groups (large-jacket negatives are numbered 1 through 183007 with numerous gaps, and small-jacket negatives are numbered 155001 through 183087 with numerous gaps), with some cross-referencing for the "overlap" numbers. For those negatives numbered between 155001 and 183081 that appear in the large-jacket group, an empty jacket appears in the small-jacket group with the notation, "Original Filed in Oversize File." There are no similar cross-reference markers, however, in the large jacket group. Most of the first 5,000 items in the large-jacket group bear the agency designation "AC" (for "Air Corps," used principally on 1930's-1940's negatives but continued, for unknown reasons, into the era of the modern U.S. Air Force). Interspersed in the file are items taken earlier and bearing the "AS" (Air Service) suffix. The rest of the large jacket entries and the entirety of the small-jacket entries bear the updated "USAF" designation. Entries in both groups are, on the whole, negatives -- the original negative submitted by an Air Force photographer, an Air Force, generated copy negative, or, in some cases, both -- although there are also widely-scattered black and white transparencies and 35mm slides. Accompanying a minority of the negatives are small contact prints (placed within or attached to the respective jackets). Most of the jackets, large and small, bear information about the place, date that the image was taken, date that the image arrived at the central depository, photographic process and format, organizational source, content description, and, increasingly after the mid-1960's, photographer. The items in this series document the activities of the U.S. Air Force and its predecessors from the earliest days of military aviation through the Vietnam War. Included are combat images relating to World War I, World War II, the Korean War, post- World War II occupations of Germany and Japan, military incidents and the Cold War. Also included are photographs of aircraft, weapons, fields and installations, tests, organizations, units, and personnel. Photographs related to the history of aviation are also included.

official_records.title: Project Blue Book Case Files on Sightings of Unidentified Flying Objects (UFOs)
official_records.creator: Department of Defense. Department of the Air Force. Air Materiel Command. Intelligence Department. Technical Intelligence Division. (1947 - 1951)
official_records.summary: This series consists of the case files on sightings of unidentified flying objects (UFOs) of Project Blue Book, the U.S. Air Force (USAF) investigation into UFOs which were sighted between June 1947 and December 1969. From 1947 through 1951, the USAF Air Material Command Intelligence Department Technical Intelligence Division maintained the series. From 1951 through March 1952, the USAF Office of the Deputy Chief of Staff Operations Office of the Director of Intelligence Air Technical Intelligence Center maintained the series. From March 1952 through 1969, the USAF Air Force Systems Command Foreign Technology Division Project Blue Book Office and its predecessors maintained the series. The first subseries contains sighting case files. The second subseries contains photographs that have been withdrawn from the first subseries. The files contain the information the Air Force gathered about specific UFO sightings. Each case file relates to one sighting or to a group of closely related sightings. The files contain reports from UFO observers, correspondence between these observers and the Air Force, newspaper and magazine clippings, and reports of analyses of photographs and physical evidence. Some reports were submitted by letter or telegram, but most reports of sightings were submitted on an Air Force questionnaire which contains the name and address of the observer, date and hour of the sighting, and a description of what the observer saw. Each case file contains a control sheet which summarizes the sighting report and shows the Air Force explanation and conclusions for the sighting. There is a monthly list of sightings of unidentified flying objects for which case files were prepared. For each sighting the list contains the date, location, name of observer, and evaluation of the sighting report. The list for each month can be found at the beginning of the relevant files in this series. The case files contain cross reference sheets to photographs that can be found in the second subseries to this series. The case files also contain cross reference sheets with citations to the photographs, motion pictures, sound recordings, and artifacts that were submitted with reports and that can be found in the series "Project 'BLUE BOOK', 1954-1966" (National Archives Identifier 542184), "Project Blue Book Motion Picture Films, 1950 - 1966" (National Archives Identifier 61934), "Sound Recordings Relating to Project Blue Book Unidentified Flying Object (UFO) Investigations, 1953 - 1967" (National Archives Identifier 1142703), and "Project Bluebook Artifacts, 1952 - 1969" (National Archives Identifier 23857160).

official_records.creator: Department of Defense. Department of the Air Force. Office of the Chief of Staff. Office of the Assistant Chief of Staff, Intelligence. Aerospace Technical Intelligence Center. (9/21/1959 - 7/1/1961)
official_records.summary: In December 1947, after the alleged sightings of flying saucers near Mt. Rainer, Washington, the Air Force, whose responsibilities include the air defense of the country, established Project Sign. Documentation for the project was created and acquired by the Aerial Phenomena Branch, Foreign Technology Division (FTD), Air Force Command (AFSC) until December 1969 when the UFO function was canceled by the Secretary of the Air Force. From 1951 through 1961, FTD was designated the Aerospace Technical Intelligence Center under Assistant Chief of Staff Intelligence (ASC/l), HQ USAF. Prior to that it was the Intelligence Department of Air Material Command. The purpose of Project Sign was to determine whether UFO's were a threat to the national security. In 1948 the project name was changed to Project Grudge and in 1952 the code name was again changed to Project Blue Book and the formal title to Aerial Phenomenon Group. The sightings were recorded by individuals (whose names were not released), by groups, and by the military. Film records of the alleged sightings were made in- Tulsa, Oklahoma; Australia; Fairchild AFB, Washington; Binghamton, NY; Naha, Okinawa; Snohomish, Washington; Almogordo, New Mexico; Montville, Ohio; Sandusky, Ohio; Olmsted AFB, PA; Keesler AFB, MS; Coburn, VA; and Edwards AFB, CA. There are 9 rolls of film of timed radar responses in the following locations- Wichita, Kansas; Macao, China; Edwards AFB, CA; Bermuda; Duluth, Minnesota; Queen Charlotte Islands, CANADA. There is a reference set of these records, consisting of contact sheets or positive rolled film.

Photographs in this series include an image of the GSFC site plan (255-GS-1428); a view of the NASA organizational chart from August 1961 (255-GS-1230); a picture of a 1962 map of Cape Canaveral, Florida (255-GS-62-3245); and construction views of the Rosman Satellite Tracking Station in Rosman, North Carolina (255-GS-63-3208 through 255-GS-63-3231). Lovell, Jr. and Buzz Aldrin posing with the spacecraft (255-GS-67-4324 through 255-GS-67-4331); and pictures relating to various Space Shuttle missions throughout the 1980s. Images relating to unmanned space missions include launch views of Mercury-Atlas 4 (MA-4) on September 13, 1961 (255-GS-62-669); pre-launch images of the Pioneer 7 space probe on August 11, 1966 (255-GS-67-4230 through 255-GS-67-4238); launch views and images of the moon taken by the Lunar Orbiter IV in May 1967 (255-GS-67-9268 through 255-GS-67-9274); and pictures taken by the Surveyor III Lander that explored the moon in April 1967 (255-GS-67-9736 through 255-GS-67-9752). Other photographs in this series include photographs relating to satellites and space telescopes, including an image of Echo I (255-GS-63-536); a launch view of the Orbiting Solar Observatory (OSO) in 1962 (255-GS-62-3096); a picture of an artist drawing of a Syncom satellite (255-GS-62-661); a view of the Intelsat II F-2 satellite being launched on January 11, 1967 (255-GS-67-4903); various mosaic images of Earth taken by Landstat satellites; and observations of Halley's Comet taken in 1985 by the International Ultraviolet Explorer (255-GS-85-5606, 255-GS-85-5607, 255-GS-85-5641 and 255-GS-85-5642). Personalities in this series include portraits of President John F. Kennedy (255-GS-1690); NASA Space Physicist Don Lind (255-GS-66-7076 to 255-GS-66-7085); Assistant Director of GSFC, E. W. Covington at his desk in November 1966 (255-GS-67-3501); and astronaut John Glenn visiting Pope Paul VI in October 1965 during the first NASA goodwill tour of Europe (255-GS-66-4472). osint_methods.summary: Track where a file came from, whether it is an official asset, a mirror, an uploaded derivative, or a social-media repost. Treat metadata loss and re-encoding as evidence-quality changes.
osint_methods.tools: source URLs, hashes, archive snapshots, original download pages

osint_methods.title: Model parallax, focus, and optical artifacts
osint_methods.summary: Small nearby objects, camera stabilization, glare, bokeh, thermal blooming, and platform motion can mimic high speed or unusual maneuvers in 2D footage.
osint_methods.tools: frame stepping, camera geometry, lens specs, background motion, independent landmarks

osint_methods.title: Separate report volume from event volume
osint_methods.summary: Crowdsourced sighting spikes can reflect media attention, internet access, reporting behavior, and database collection practices rather than changes in phenomena.
osint_methods.tools: date normalization, population controls, media event timelines, duplicate detection

osint_methods.title: Document sensor and platform context
osint_methods.summary: For video or imagery, record camera type, field of view, platform motion, frame rate, compression, overlays, timestamp, pointing angle, and any missing telemetry before estimating object behavior.
osint_methods.tools: DVIDS/AARO descriptions, video overlays, EXIF/metadata, frame extraction

osint_methods.title: Compare prosaic morphology
osint_methods.summary: Resolved cases often turn on morphology, wind correlation, wings/balloon movement, thermal signature, or motion consistent with birds, balloons, aircraft, or airborne debris.
osint_methods.tools: wind profiles, NOAA weather, visual comparison libraries, AARO resolved-case reports
